Case A

A1. The seven-day search returned only the earlier requests, so no earlier misuse is visible in that window. The key was published at some earlier time, though, and the search covered only seven days. It also says nothing about requests that were not logged under this key. Whether the burst was the first misuse can't be determined. The burst came 19 minutes after publication, and the earlier requests look like the legitimate client. But the window might not reach back to publication, and "past seven days" is probably measured from the scan, which could be well after publication. Cannot tell.

A2. We don't know what evidence the check had or what it was looking for. The burst, the payout change and the shared destination were all available in principle, but the check's inputs and thresholds are not shown. Cannot tell.

A3. A shared payout destination could mean one owner, but it could also be a payment processor, a shared business bank account, or a family arrangement. The answer is No, not by itself.

A4. No reports after 30 days is weak evidence at best, and victims may not have noticed or reported. If the payouts were fraudulent, the victim might be the account owner, who may not have looked. The options are "Yes, weakly", "No" and "Cannot tell". Absence of a report doesn't indicate legitimacy, because no one may be looking or the account holder may be the one who was compromised. I'll choose No.

A5. Yes. The burst involved a changed fingerprint, a residential proxy, and a payout destination change right after the key was published.

Case B

B1. D has 0 chargebacks against 2 at each of the others, with 100 transactions each, so its recorded rate is lower: 0% against 2%. Yes.

B2. The combined 5 percent is a pooled figure and says nothing about individual accounts. The measure is chargeback-or-alert, and it is higher than the chargeback counts alone, which total 6 of 400, or 1.5%. The pooled figure could hide an account above 5 percent. No.

B3. The search found no accounts beyond A and the closed account, but it only covers the identifiers searched. It doesn't rule out accounts under other names. Also, the search "across all merchant accounts" found A and the closed account, and says nothing about B to D's controllers. Cannot tell.

B4. Two notes from different analysts on different days may still rest on the same evidence, and we don't know whether they worked independently. Cannot tell.

B5. A blocked payment is a suspected fraud attempt, and the lack of a chargeback is expected because it was blocked. No.

B6. Shared templates and descriptor patterns justify looking at them together. Yes.

RESULT CN-081 | A1: Cannot tell | A2: Cannot tell | A3: No, not by itself | A4: No | A5: Yes | B1: Yes | B2: No | B3: Cannot tell | B4: Cannot tell | B5: No | B6: Yes
